ev.ind_g_bakhtiyar.title: Eighteen horsemen
ev.ind_g_bakhtiyar.text: They say just eighteen horsemen rode into the capital Nadia disguised as horse dealers, and old King Lakshmanasena fled by the back gate. Then came the army of the Turk Bakhtiyar Khalji. The new masters are taking the palaces and the taxes.
ev.ind_g_bakhtiyar.note: Around 1204 Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji took Nadia, the residence of the Bengal king Lakshmanasena of the Sena dynasty, in a surprise raid. The Senas ruled in eastern Bengal for some decades more, while in the west a Muslim domain arose with its capital at Lakhnauti (Gaur).
ev.ind_g_bakhtiyar.east: Go east, to the Sena lands
ev.ind_g_sultanate.title: A new sultan
ev.ind_g_sultanate.text: Heralds announced in the bazaars that Qutb al-Din Aibak, once a slave and a general of the Ghurid sultan, now rules in his own right from Delhi and Lahore. Taxes go to him; the Friday sermon is read in his name.
ev.ind_g_sultanate.note: After Muhammad of Ghur was killed in 1206, his governor in India, Qutb al-Din Aibak, a former ghulam, became an independent ruler in all but name. This is the conventional start of the Delhi Sultanate, which lasted until 1526.
ev.ind_g_qutb.title: The victory tower
ev.ind_g_qutb.text: By the new mosque in Delhi a huge tower of red sandstone is going up. There aren't enough masons, carvers and porters, and they pay by the day. The stone comes from dismantled temples.
ev.ind_g_qutb.note: The Qutb Minar was begun under Aibak around 1199 and completed by Iltutmish. Beside it stands the Quwwat al-Islam mosque, built with pillars taken from dismantled Hindu and Jain temples.
ev.ind_g_genghis.title: Mongols on the Indus
ev.ind_g_genghis.text: People are fleeing from the west: the Mongol khan Genghis has crushed the Shah of Khwarazm right on the banks of the Indus. The shah's son begs Sultan Iltutmish for refuge, but he politely declines - no one wants to draw the Mongol hordes to Delhi.
ev.ind_g_genghis.note: In 1221 Genghis Khan defeated Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah at the Battle of the Indus. Iltutmish refused the fugitive refuge, and the Mongols did not then push deeper into India, though their raids on the northwest went on for another century.
ev.ind_g_razia.title: Sultan Razia
ev.ind_g_razia.text: Iltutmish's daughter Razia has taken the throne. She rides an elephant unveiled, in a coat and turban, hears petitions herself and leads the army. The nobles grumble, and in the bazaar people argue: can a woman rule?
ev.ind_g_razia.note: Razia (r. 1236–1240) was the only woman to sit on the throne of the Delhi Sultanate. Her father named her heir over his sons. She ruled firmly, but the nobles known as "the Forty" rebelled, and Razia was killed in 1240.
ev.ind_g_jagadu.title: Jagadu's granaries
ev.ind_g_jagadu.text: Three years without rain, and Gujarat is starving. The Jain merchant Jagadu has thrown open his granaries and hands out grain to all comers - Hindus, Jains and Muslims alike. They say he bought up grain in advance, foreseeing the drought.
ev.ind_g_jagadu.note: Jagadu Shah was a Jain merchant of Bhadreshwar in Kutch. According to later biographies, during the famine of 1256–1258 he distributed grain from his granaries across Gujarat and neighbouring lands. The legend has been embellished, but the famine and the merchant's generosity appear in many sources.
ev.ind_g_mongol_siege.title: Mongols at the walls
ev.ind_g_mongol_siege.text: A huge Mongol army has come right up to Delhi. The villages around are burning, the gates are shut, and the city is running out of grain. Sultan Alauddin holds his camp at Siri and will not be lured into the open field.
ev.ind_g_mongol_siege.note: In 1299 (the battle of Kili) and in 1303 Chagatai Mongols advanced to Delhi. Alauddin Khalji repulsed them and fortified the frontier, and to pay for his vast army he introduced his famous market reforms.
ev.ind_g_mongol_siege.fields: Wait it out in the far fields
ev.ind_g_mongol_siege.fields.success: The Mongol patrols passed you by.
ev.ind_g_mongol_siege.fields.failure: A patrol stumbled on you. They took everything you had.
ev.ind_g_khalji_gujarat.title: Alauddin's army
ev.ind_g_khalji_gujarat.text: The army of Sultan Alauddin of Delhi has entered Gujarat. Raja Karna has fled, the temple of Somnath has been plundered, and in Cambay gold and slaves are being taken from the rich merchants. They say among the captives is a handsome young eunuch, bought for the sultan for a thousand dinars.
ev.ind_g_khalji_gujarat.note: In 1299 Alauddin Khalji's generals conquered Gujarat, overthrowing Karna, the last raja of the Vaghela dynasty, and plundered the Somnath temple. At Cambay they bought the slave Malik Kafur, who later became the sultan's chief general.
ev.ind_g_markets.title: The sultan's prices
ev.ind_g_markets.text: Sultan Alauddin has fixed the prices of grain, cloth, horses and even slaves. Inspectors walk the rows with scales, and spies send children to the bazaar to see if anyone short-weights a little one. Bread has never been so cheap, but cheating is punished so harshly that the whole bazaar flinches afterwards.
ev.ind_g_markets.note: Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296–1316) imposed price controls in Delhi: the state collected tax in grain for its granaries, merchants were registered, and short weight was cruelly punished. The chronicler Barani writes that prices stayed the same for as long as the sultan lived.
ev.ind_g_markets.cheat.success: You sold under the counter at a good profit, and no one noticed.
ev.ind_g_markets.cheat.failure: An inspector caught you giving short weight. The punishment was harsh, and your goods went to the treasury.
ev.ind_g_daulatabad.title: To Daulatabad!
ev.ind_g_daulatabad.text: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq has ordered the capital moved forty days' march south, to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad. Nobles, scholars and craftsmen must go there with all their belongings. Shelters and wells have been set up along the road, but people still collapse from the heat.
ev.ind_g_daulatabad.note: In 1327 Muhammad bin Tughluq moved his capital to Daulatabad in the Deccan to govern the south better, and forced Delhi's elite to resettle there. A few years later the capital was moved back, and many never made it home.
ev.ind_g_daulatabad.hide.success: They did not find you. The city is empty, but you are home.
ev.ind_g_daulatabad.hide.failure: The kotwal's men found you. You had to pay them off and go anyway.
ev.ind_g_token.title: Copper tankas
ev.ind_g_token.text: The sultan has decreed that copper and brass coins shall pass at par with silver. Now every household is minting "coins" right at the hearth, merchants refuse copper, and prices jump every day.
ev.ind_g_token.note: Around 1329–1332 Muhammad bin Tughluq issued "token" coins of copper and brass with the face value of silver. They were easy to forge, and the country was soon flooded with fakes. The sultan cancelled the reform and redeemed the copper with silver from the treasury.
ev.ind_g_token.tokens: Take the copper - what else can you do
ev.ind_g_token.silver: Hide your silver and sell nothing
ev.ind_g_token.forge.success: Your coppers are as good as the treasury's. As long as people take them, you're ahead.
ev.ind_g_token.forge.failure: A neighbour informed on you. You had to pay off the watch with everything you had.
ev.ind_g_famine_1335.title: The hungry years
ev.ind_g_famine_1335.text: The rains have failed for several years running, yet the taxes have not been lowered. The villages around Delhi are emptying as people flee to the forests. The sultan hands out loans to farmers for seed and wells, and has himself moved his camp east to the Ganges, where there is still grain.
ev.ind_g_famine_1335.note: In the 1330s a terrible drought and famine struck the Doab and the country around Delhi. Muhammad bin Tughluq gave farmers state loans (sondhar) and for a time moved his court to the camp of Sargadwari on the Ganges.
ev.ind_g_vijaya_found.title: City of Victory
ev.ind_g_vijaya_found.text: The brothers Harihara and Bukka have founded a new capital on the banks of the Tungabhadra - Vijayanagara, the City of Victory. People say the sage Vidyaranya showed them the place, and here an empire will rise that will stop the sultans.
ev.ind_g_vijaya_found.note: The Vijayanagara empire was founded around 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty. Tradition links its founding to the sage Vidyaranya. For over two centuries the empire united the south of India.
ev.ind_g_ilyas.title: The Bengal sultan
ev.ind_g_ilyas.text: Ilyas Shah has united all of Bengal and calls himself sultan. Firuz Shah of Delhi has come to punish the rebel, but Ilyas has shut himself in the fortress of Ekdala among the rivers and swamps. The rains will soon begin, and the men from Delhi are nervous.
ev.ind_g_ilyas.note: Shams al-Din Ilyas Shah had united Bengal into an independent sultanate by 1352. Firuz Shah Tughluq's campaign of 1353–1354 came to nothing: Ilyas held out at Ekdala, and Bengal remained independent for two hundred years.
ev.ind_g_bahmani_war.title: The war for the Raichur doab
ev.ind_g_bahmani_war.text: War again with the Bahmani Sultanate over the fertile lands between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra. The sultan's cavalry burns the villages, and the raya's army marches to meet it.
ev.ind_g_bahmani_war.note: The Bahmani Sultanate (founded 1347) and Vijayanagara fought for almost two hundred years over the Raichur doab, the land between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra. The wars swung back and forth and devastated the borderlands.
ev.ind_g_bahmani_war.serve.success: You came back with plunder and stories for a lifetime.
ev.ind_g_bahmani_war.serve.failure: You were badly wounded in the fighting at the ford.
ev.ind_g_bahmani_war.shelter: Shelter the family in a fortress
ev.ind_g_firuz.title: Firuz Shah's canals
ev.ind_g_firuz.text: Sultan Firuz Shah is digging canals from the Yamuna, planting gardens and building a new city, Firozabad, with a hospital that treats people for free, and even an office that finds work for the unemployed. They say he had an ancient pillar covered in unreadable writing brought to Delhi.
ev.ind_g_firuz.note: Firuz Shah Tughluq (r. 1351–1388) built canals, gardens, towns and hospitals. He had two pillars of the emperor Ashoka (3rd century BC) brought to Delhi; no one at the time could read their inscriptions.
ev.ind_g_firuz.canal: Hire on to dig the canal
ev.ind_g_durga_devi.title: The Durga Devi famine
ev.ind_g_durga_devi.text: No rain, year after year. The fields have cracked, and people eat roots and bark. The temples hand out gruel from their storehouses, but the queues stretch to the horizon.
ev.ind_g_durga_devi.note: Tradition and later chronicles speak of a terrible twelve-year famine, the "Durga Devi", in the Deccan in the late 14th and early 15th centuries. Historians dispute its exact dates and scale.
ev.ind_g_durga_devi.temple: Go to the temple for gruel
ev.ind_g_timur.title: Timur
ev.ind_g_timur.text: The lame emir Timur of Samarkand has routed the sultan's army beneath the walls of Delhi. The city surrendered, but his soldiers began to plunder and everything slipped out of control. Fires can be seen from everywhere, and craftsmen are being led away to Samarkand to build mosques.
ev.ind_g_timur.note: In December 1398 Timur defeated the army of the last Tughluqs and took Delhi. The city was sacked, many inhabitants were killed, and thousands of craftsmen were carried off to Central Asia. Delhi took a long time to recover.
ev.ind_g_timur.flee: Flee the city while you can
ev.ind_g_timur.hide.success: You stayed in the dark for three days. When you came out the house was empty, but you were alive.
ev.ind_g_timur.hide.failure: They found you. By some miracle you survived, but you lost almost everything.
ev.ind_g_china_fleet.title: Envoys from China
ev.ind_g_china_fleet.text: Huge ships from China with coloured sails have anchored in the river mouth. The emperor's envoys have brought silk and porcelain, and the sultan is sending gifts in return - they say even a live giraffe brought from Africa.
ev.ind_g_china_fleet.note: The fleets of the Chinese admiral Zheng He visited Bengal between 1405 and 1433. In 1414 an embassy from the Bengal sultan brought a giraffe to Beijing, which the Ming court took for the fabulous qilin.
ev.ind_g_ahmedabad.title: A new capital
ev.ind_g_ahmedabad.text: Sultan Ahmad Shah is founding a new city on the banks of the Sabarmati - Ahmedabad. Merchants and craftsmen are invited to settle there with privileges, and each community gets its own gated quarter, a pol.
ev.ind_g_ahmedabad.note: Ahmedabad was founded in 1411 by Sultan Ahmad Shah I as the new capital of the Gujarat Sultanate. It quickly became one of the greatest trading and craft centres of India.
ev.ind_g_bengali_epic.title: The Mahabharata in Bengali
ev.ind_g_bengali_epic.text: In the governor's courtyard a reciter declaims the Mahabharata - not in Sanskrit, but in Bengali that everyone understands. A general of the Muslim sultan commissioned the translation. The listeners weep over the fate of the Pandavas.
ev.ind_g_bengali_epic.note: Under Sultan Alauddin Husain Shah (r. 1494–1519) and his successors Bengali literature flourished. His generals Paragal Khan and Chhuti Khan commissioned translations of the Mahabharata into Bengali.
ev.ind_g_diu.title: The battle of Diu
ev.ind_g_diu.text: Off the island of Diu the ships of Governor Malik Ayaz and an Egyptian Mamluk fleet have gathered to drive off the Portuguese. The guns roar so loudly they can be heard in the town.
ev.ind_g_diu.note: In February 1509 the Portuguese fleet of Francisco de Almeida defeated the combined forces of the Gujarat Sultanate, Mamluk Egypt and Calicut off Diu. The victory made the Portuguese masters of the seas around India for a long time.
ev.ind_g_diu.row: Row on one of Malik Ayaz's ships
ev.ind_g_diu.row.success: Your ship survived. You came back with your pay and a few grey hairs.
ev.ind_g_diu.row.failure: A cannonball smashed the hull. You were fished out of the water wounded.
ev.ind_g_goa.title: Firangis at Goa
ev.ind_g_goa.text: The Portuguese have taken the port of Goa from the sultan of Bijapur. Now the Arab horses reach the raya through their hands, and Portuguese envoys have become frequent visitors at Krishnadevaraya's court.
ev.ind_g_goa.note: In 1510 Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate. The Portuguese became the main suppliers of warhorses to Vijayanagara, and Krishnadevaraya kept on friendly terms with them.
ev.ind_g_goa.trade.success: Cloth and spices went to Goa at a fine profit.
ev.ind_g_goa.trade.failure: A Portuguese factor cheated you on the price.
ev.ind_g_raichur.title: Victory at Raichur
ev.ind_g_raichur.text: The great raya Krishnadevaraya has taken the fortress of Raichur, routing the army of the sultan of Bijapur. The capital celebrates for a week, sweets are handed out in the bazaars, and poets compose verses on the victory.
ev.ind_g_raichur.note: In 1520 Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529) defeated Ismail Adil Shah of Bijapur and took Raichur. His reign is considered the golden age of Vijayanagara, when Telugu and Kannada poetry and temple building flourished.
ev.ind_g_panipat.title: Guns at Panipat
ev.ind_g_panipat.text: Babur, an outsider who rules in Kabul, has defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi's huge army at Panipat. Babur has few men, but he has cannon and muskets, and the sultan's elephants went mad at the noise. The sultan is dead, and Babur has proclaimed himself padishah.
ev.ind_g_panipat.note: In April 1526 Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the first battle of Panipat, using field artillery and muskets. So began the empire of the Great Mughals.
ev.ind_g_panipat.welcome: Hope for a change for the better
ev.ind_g_humayun_gujarat.title: Turmoil in Gujarat
ev.ind_g_humayun_gujarat.text: The Mughal padishah Humayun has taken the fortress of Champaner, and Sultan Bahadur Shah fled to the coast and gave Diu to the Portuguese in exchange for help. Soon after came the news that the sultan drowned after a meeting aboard a Portuguese ship.
ev.ind_g_humayun_gujarat.note: In 1535 Humayun defeated Bahadur Shah of Gujarat and took Champaner. Bahadur ceded Diu to the Portuguese and in 1537 died during negotiations aboard one of their ships. The Mughals soon withdrew from Gujarat.
ev.ind_g_sher_shah_bengal.title: Sher Khan takes Gaur
ev.ind_g_sher_shah_bengal.text: The Afghan Sher Khan has taken and plundered Gaur, and the Bengal sultan has fled. Then came the Mughal padishah Humayun, and then Sher Khan defeated him at Chausa. Armies march back and forth, and each one takes its share.
ev.ind_g_sher_shah_bengal.note: In 1538 Sher Khan Sur seized Gaur, and in 1539 he defeated Humayun at Chausa and proclaimed himself Sher Shah. After the battle of Kannauj in 1540 Humayun fled India.
ev.ind_g_sher_shah_road.title: Sher Shah's road
ev.ind_g_sher_shah_road.text: Sher Shah is laying a great road from Bengal to the Indus, with trees along the verges, wells and caravanserais every few kos where Hindus and Muslims alike are fed. His new silver coin, the rupee, is in circulation.
ev.ind_g_sher_shah_road.note: Sher Shah Suri (r. 1540–1545) restored and improved the great road from Sonargaon in Bengal to the Punjab, built hundreds of sarais and introduced the silver rupee, which became the basis of Indian currency for centuries.
ev.ind_g_panipat2.title: Famine and Panipat
ev.ind_g_panipat2.text: Crop failure and war have come in the same year: grain costs ten times its price, and people are dying on the roads. Hemu, a Hindu minister of the Afghan sultans, has taken Delhi, and the young padishah Akbar is marching to meet him at Panipat.
ev.ind_g_panipat2.note: In 1555–1556 a terrible famine struck the country around Agra and Delhi. In November 1556, at the second battle of Panipat, the forces of Akbar and his regent Bairam Khan defeated Hemu, who had been struck in the eye by an arrow.
ev.ind_g_jizya_end.title: Akbar abolishes the jizya
ev.ind_g_jizya_end.text: The heralds have announced that Padishah Akbar has abolished the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims, and the pilgrim toll the year before. In the bazaar people can't believe it, ask each other again and again, and bless the young sovereign.
ev.ind_g_jizya_end.note: In 1563 Akbar abolished the pilgrim tax, and in 1564 the jizya. These measures became part of his policy of sulh-i kul, "peace with all".
ev.ind_g_talikota.title: The sack
ev.ind_g_talikota.text: At Talikota the combined armies of the Deccan sultans have routed the raya's army; the regent Rama Raya is dead. The court is fleeing south with the treasury on hundreds of elephants, and the victors are entering the defenceless city. Smoke rises over the City of Victory.
ev.ind_g_talikota.note: In January 1565 a coalition of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara at the battle of Talikota (Rakkasa-Tangadi). The regent Rama Raya was killed, and the capital was plundered and destroyed over several months. The empire survived, but its centre moved south to Penukonda and Chandragiri.
ev.ind_g_talikota.village: Go to your kin in the village
ev.ind_g_talikota.stay.success: You survived the sack hidden in a temple's stone storeroom. The city is gone.
ev.ind_g_talikota.stay.failure: Plunderers burst into the house. You survived by a miracle, but lost everything.
ev.ind_g_fatehpur.title: Akbar's City of Victory
ev.ind_g_fatehpur.text: Near Sikri, where the Sufi Shaykh Salim Chishti he reveres lives, the padishah is building a whole new city of red stone. There are not enough stonecutters, carvers and carpenters, and in the House of Worship Muslim ulama, brahmins, Jains, Parsis and even Portuguese friars debate.
ev.ind_g_fatehpur.note: Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri between 1571 and 1585. From 1575 his Ibadat Khana, the House of Worship, hosted debates between scholars of different faiths. Because of water shortages the court soon abandoned the city.
ev.ind_g_fatehpur.work: Hire on at the building site
ev.ind_g_akbar_gujarat.title: Akbar in Gujarat
ev.ind_g_akbar_gujarat.text: Padishah Akbar's army has entered Gujarat, taken Ahmedabad and besieged Surat. When rebels rose again, Akbar raced down from Agra in nine days and crushed them. The Gujarat Sultanate is no more.
ev.ind_g_akbar_gujarat.note: In 1572–1573 Akbar conquered Gujarat. His lightning ride from Fatehpur Sikri to Ahmedabad in 1573 became legendary. Gujarat, with its ports, became the richest Mughal province.
ev.ind_g_akbar_gujarat.hide: Hide your goods from the soldiers
ev.ind_g_gaur_plague.title: Pestilence in Gaur
ev.ind_g_gaur_plague.text: In the old capital of Gaur, which the Mughals have just entered, a terrible disease has broken out. The river has drawn away from the city, water rots in the canals, and thousands are dying, soldiers and townspeople alike. People are fleeing without looking back.
ev.ind_g_gaur_plague.note: In 1575, shortly after Mughal troops occupied Gaur, an epidemic struck the city, killing a great many people including the general Munim Khan. The Ganges had shifted its course by then, and Gaur was abandoned for good.
ev.ind_g_gaur_plague.stay.success: The disease passed your house by.
ev.ind_g_mughal_bengal.title: The Mughals and the twelve chiefs
ev.ind_g_mughal_bengal.text: Daud Khan, the last Afghan sultan of Bengal, has fallen at Rajmahal. The Mughals send their governors, but in the east, in the delta, twelve local chiefs, the bhuiyans, refuse to recognise the padishah and fight on the rivers with fleets of boats.
ev.ind_g_mughal_bengal.note: In 1576 Daud Khan Karrani was defeated and executed, and Bengal became part of the Mughal empire. Yet the bhuiyans ("twelve chiefs"), led by Isa Khan, resisted Mughal rule in eastern Bengal for decades.
ev.ind_g_din_ilahi.title: The divine faith
ev.ind_g_din_ilahi.text: They say Padishah Akbar has gathered chosen disciples around him and created his own path, the Din-i Ilahi, the "divine faith": reverence for the sun and fire, one God, peace with all religions. The ulama are outraged, the brahmins cautiously pleased, and ordinary people simply wonder.
ev.ind_g_din_ilahi.note: Around 1582 Akbar founded the Din-i Ilahi, a circle of courtiers bound by personal loyalty to the padishah and a teaching that combined elements of different religions. It had very few followers and faded after Akbar's death in 1605.
ev.ind_g_din_ilahi.approve: Peace among all faiths is right
ev.ind_g_din_ilahi.doubt: It is not for a sovereign to change faith
ev.ind_g_nayakas.title: Every nayaka for himself
ev.ind_g_nayakas.text: The raya now rules from distant Penukonda, then from Chandragiri, and his word weighs less and less. The nayakas, the war lords of Mysore, Madurai and Thanjavur, collect taxes and mint coins on their own. The taxes are still taken; it is just unclear by whom.
ev.ind_g_nayakas.note: After 1565 the Aravidu dynasty ruled the remnants of the empire from Penukonda and Chandragiri. The nayakas of Madurai, Thanjavur and Keladi and the rulers of Mysore (who took Srirangapatna in 1610) gradually became independent.
ev.ind_g_arakan_raids.title: Boats from Arakan
ev.ind_g_arakan_raids.text: At night swift boats of the Arakanese "Maghs" and Portuguese pirates from Chittagong come up the rivers. They burn villages and carry people off to be sold. The river lands are emptying.
ev.ind_g_arakan_raids.note: In the first half of the seventeenth century fleets from Arakan and Portuguese adventurers from Chittagong ravaged lower Bengal, seizing people to sell as slaves. The raids were ended by the Mughal governor Shaista Khan, who took Chittagong in 1666.
ev.ind_g_arakan_raids.hide.success: The boats passed by. In the morning you went back to your house, still standing.
ev.ind_g_arakan_raids.hide.failure: The pirates burned the house and took everything they found.
ev.ind_g_famine_1630.title: The great famine
ev.ind_g_famine_1630.text: Two years without rain, and then downpours that washed the crops away. The villages of Gujarat are dying out, people lie along the roads, and in Surat the merchants see things they will never forget. Padishah Shah Jahan has ordered free kitchens opened.
ev.ind_g_famine_1630.note: The famine of 1630–1632 in Gujarat and the Deccan was one of the worst disasters of the seventeenth century. Contemporaries, including Dutch and English merchants in Surat, wrote of millions dead. Shah Jahan opened free kitchens and reduced taxes.
ev.ind_g_famine_1630.give: Hand out grain from your own stores
ev.ind_g_shahjahanabad.title: A new Delhi
ev.ind_g_shahjahanabad.text: Padishah Shah Jahan is building a new capital on the Yamuna, Shahjahanabad: the Red Fort, the broad Chandni Chowk with a canal down its middle, and a huge Friday mosque. The court is returning from Agra, and Delhi is coming back to life.
ev.ind_g_shahjahanabad.note: Shahjahanabad was built between 1639 and 1648. The Red Fort and the Jama Masjid became symbols of Delhi, and Chandni Chowk its main market street.
ev.ind_g_shahjahanabad.work: Hire on at the building site
ev.ind_g_shahjahanabad.look: Go and watch the city grow
